slides.text:
A `for` loop runs its block once for every value of a sequence. The sequence you will use most is a **range** of numbers, and an array is another one.

You will write ranges that stop before the end or include it, reshape them to count down or skip, and loop over the elements of an array.
Pseudo code, not Rust. The loop takes the values one by one, and the block sees one value at a time.
A range is written `start..end`. It begins at `start` and stops **before** `end`. The loop variable is a new name on each pass, and it only exists inside the loop.
Add an `=` to include the end. Pseudo code, not Rust.
When the number itself is not needed, name the variable `_` and the loop only repeats the block.

slides.text: A range is a value with methods. `.rev()` walks it backwards and `.step_by(n)` moves `n` at a time. Put the range in parentheses so the method applies to all of it. Methods like these are called adapters, and they get their own course later. Pseudo code, not Rust.

A range only counts up. When the start is already past the end, the range is empty and the loop body never runs. To count down, reverse a range that counts up.

Ranges also work on `char` values, letter by letter.

slides.text: A `for` can walk the elements of an array directly, with no index. When you need the position, loop over the indexes with a range instead: `0..array.len()`.
The loop variable is an ordinary value inside the block, so it can feed a calculation on every pass, and a `for` can sit inside another `for`.
